title: Fire Commanders Who Do Not Compare Options
text:
In the mid-1980s the psychologist Gary Klein and his colleagues Roberta Calderwood and Anne Clinton-Cirocco set out to study how experienced fire commanders make life-and-death decisions under time pressure. They expected to find that commanders compared a few options and picked the best, as textbooks on decision making recommended.

They interviewed veteran fireground commanders in the United States about difficult incidents they had handled, going through each fire step by step and asking what the commanders had noticed and what they had considered at every decision point.

The commanders insisted they rarely compared options at all. In the large majority of decisions, they recognized the situation as a familiar type, and that recognition immediately suggested a reasonable course of action. Before acting, they often ran it forward in their minds, imagining how it would play out. If the mental simulation revealed a problem, they modified the plan or moved to the next option that came to mind. They did not lay out alternatives side by side.

Klein called this recognition-primed decision making. In a case Klein later retold in his book Sources of Power, a lieutenant ordered his crew out of a burning house because the fire felt wrong: too hot and too quiet. The floor collapsed soon after. The fire had been in the basement beneath them. The work launched the field of naturalistic decision making, the study of how experts actually decide in real settings.
lesson: Experience lets you recognize what a situation calls for and act quickly. Before you commit, run the plan forward in your mind, and if something feels off, take that signal seriously.
people: Gary Klein, Roberta Calderwood, Anne Clinton-Cirocco
source: Klein, G. A., Calderwood, R., and Clinton-Cirocco, A. (1986). Rapid decision making on the fire ground. Proceedings of the Human Factors Society 30th Annual Meeting.
